claim: LXG proteins belong to a polymorphic toxin family present in Streptococcus intermedius.
source: Here we show that proteins belonging to the LXG polymorphic toxin family present in Streptococcus intermedius mediate cell contact- and Esx secretion pathway-dependent growth inhibition of diverse Firmicute species.
evidence: The abstract directly states that LXG proteins are present in S. intermedius and belong to a polymorphic toxin family.

claim: LXG proteins mediate cell contact-dependent growth inhibition of diverse Firmicute species.
source: Here we show that proteins belonging to the LXG polymorphic toxin family present in Streptococcus intermedius mediate cell contact- and Esx secretion pathway-dependent growth inhibition of diverse Firmicute species.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that LXG proteins mediate cell contact-dependent growth inhibition, supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: LXG proteins mediate Esx secretion pathway-dependent growth inhibition of diverse Firmicute species.
source: Here we show that proteins belonging to the LXG polymorphic toxin family present in Streptococcus intermedius mediate cell contact- and Esx secretion pathway-dependent growth inhibition of diverse Firmicute species.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that LXG proteins mediate Esx secretion pathway-dependent growth inhibition, supported by experimental data showing essC-dependent secretion.

claim: One LXG toxin has a previously unobserved protein fold.
source: The structure of one such toxin revealed a previously unobserved protein fold that we demonstrate directs the degradation of a uniquely bacterial molecule required for cell wall biosynthesis, lipid II.
evidence: The abstract states that the structure revealed a previously unobserved fold, supported by crystallographic data in the manuscript.

claim: TelC directs the degradation of lipid II.
source: The structure of one such toxin revealed a previously unobserved protein fold that we demonstrate directs the degradation of a uniquely bacterial molecule required for cell wall biosynthesis, lipid II.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that the toxin degrades lipid II, supported by biochemical assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: Lipid II is a uniquely bacterial molecule required for cell wall biosynthesis.
source: The structure of one such toxin revealed a previously unobserved protein fold that we demonstrate directs the degradation of a uniquely bacterial molecule required for cell wall biosynthesis, lipid II.
evidence: The abstract characterizes lipid II as uniquely bacterial and required for cell wall biosynthesis, drawing on established scientific knowledge.

claim: LXG genes are prevalent in the human gut microbiome.
source: Consistent with our functional data linking LXG toxins to interbacterial interactions in S. intermedius, we show that LXG genes are prevalent in the human gut microbiome, a polymicrobial community dominated by Firmicutes.
evidence: The abstract states that LXG genes are prevalent in the human gut microbiome, supported by metagenomic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The human gut microbiome is a polymicrobial community dominated by Firmicutes.
source: Consistent with our functional data linking LXG toxins to interbacterial interactions in S. intermedius, we show that LXG genes are prevalent in the human gut microbiome, a polymicrobial community dominated by Firmicutes.
evidence: The abstract characterizes the human gut microbiome as dominated by Firmicutes, drawing on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Interbacterial antagonism mediated by LXG toxins plays a critical role in shaping Firmicute-rich bacterial communities.
source: We speculate that interbacterial antagonism mediated by LXG toxins plays a critical role in shaping Firmicute-rich bacterial communities.
evidence: The abstract explicitly speculates about the role of LXG toxins in shaping bacterial communities based on the functional data presented.

claim: Proteobacteria widely employ contact-dependent inhibition (CDI) to intoxicate competitor cells that share a high degree of phylogenetic relatedness.
source: For instance, Proteobacteria widely employ contact-dependent inhibition (CDI) to intoxicate competitor cells that share a high degree of phylogenetic relatedness (Hayes et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites Hayes et al., 2014 to support the statement about CDI in Proteobacteria.

claim: Proteobacteria and Bacteroidetes deliver toxins to competitor Gram-negative cells through the type VI secretion system (T6SS).
source: Additionally, both Proteobacteria and bacteria belonging to the divergent phylum Bacteroidetes deliver toxins to competitor Gram-negative cells in an indiscriminate fashion through the type VI secretion system (T6SS) (Russell et al., 2014a, 2014b).
evidence: The introduction cites Russell et al., 2014a, 2014b to support the statement about T6SS-mediated toxin delivery.

claim: Cells harboring CDI or T6SS pathways prohibit self-intoxication with immunity proteins that selectively inactivate cognate toxins through direct binding.
source: Although toxin delivery by CDI and the T6SS is mechanistically distinct, cells harboring either pathway share the feature of prohibiting self-intoxication with immunity proteins that selectively inactivate cognate toxins through direct binding.
evidence: The introduction states this as a general feature of these systems, drawing on established knowledge in the field.

claim: YD-repeat family proteins in Bacillus subtilis inhibit the growth of contacting cells belonging to the same strain.
source: In Bacillus subtilis, Sec-exported proteins belonging to the YD-repeat family have been shown to potently inhibit the growth of contacting cells belonging to the same strain (Koskiniemi et al., 2013)
evidence: The introduction cites Koskiniemi et al., 2013 to support the statement about YD-repeat proteins in B. subtilis.

claim: A pathway that mediates interspecies antagonism between Gram-positive bacteria has not been identified prior to this study.
source: however, to our knowledge, a pathway that mediates interspecies antagonism between Gram-positive bacteria has not been identified.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states that no such pathway was known before this work.

claim: The Esx pathway is widely distributed among Gram-positive bacteria.
source: A specialized secretion system widely distributed among Gram-positive bacteria is the Esx pathway (also referred to as type VII secretion) (Abdallah et al., 2007).
evidence: The introduction cites Abdallah et al., 2007 to support the statement about Esx pathway distribution.

claim: The Esx pathway was first identified in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, where it plays a critical role in virulence.
source: This pathway was first identified in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, where it plays a critical role in virulence (Stanley et al., 2003).
evidence: The introduction cites Stanley et al., 2003 to support the statement about Esx pathway identification and role in M. tuberculosis.

claim: Attenuation of the vaccine strain M. bovis BCG can be attributed to a deletion inactivating ESX-1 secretion system.
source: Indeed, attenuation of the vaccine strain M. bovis BCG can be attributed to a deletion inactivating ESX-1 secretion system present in virulence strains (Lewis et al., 2003; Pym et al., 2003).
evidence: The introduction cites Lewis et al., 2003 and Pym et al., 2003 to support the statement about BCG attenuation.

claim: The Esx pathway is widely distributed in Actinobacteria.
source: Subsequent genomic studies revealed that the Esx pathway is widely distributed in Actinobacteria, and that a divergent form is present in Firmicutes (Gey Van Pittius et al., 2001; Pallen, 2002).
evidence: The introduction cites Gey Van Pittius et al., 2001 and Pallen, 2002 to support the statement about Esx pathway distribution.

claim: A divergent form of the Esx pathway is present in Firmicutes.
source: Subsequent genomic studies revealed that the Esx pathway is widely distributed in Actinobacteria, and that a divergent form is present in Firmicutes (Gey Van Pittius et al., 2001; Pallen, 2002).
evidence: The introduction cites Gey Van Pittius et al., 2001 and Pallen, 2002 to support the statement about divergent Esx pathway in Firmicutes.

claim: All Esx pathways utilize a characteristic FtsK-like AAA+ ATPase referred to as EssC (or EccC) to catalyze the export of WXG100 protein family substrates.
source: Though they share little genetic similarity, all Esx pathways studied to-date utilize a characteristic FtsK-like AAA+ ATPase referred to as EssC (or EccC) to catalyze the export of one or more substrates belonging to the WXG100 protein family (Ates et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites Ates et al., 2016 to support the statement about EssC and WXG100 substrates.

claim: WXG100 proteins, including ESAT-6 (EsxA) and CFP10 (EsxB) from M. tuberculosis, heterodimerize in order to transit the secretion machinery.
source: Proteins in this family, including ESAT-6 (EsxA) and CFP10 (EsxB) from M. tuberculosis, heterodimerize in order to transit the secretion machinery.
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge about WXG100 proteins.

claim: ESX-3 of M. tuberculosis is required for mycobactin siderophore-based iron acquisition.
source: Supporting this notion, ESX-3 of M. tuberculosis is required for mycobactin siderophore-based iron acquisition and the ESX-1 and ESX-4 systems of M. smegmatis are linked to DNA transfer (Gray et al., 2016; Siegrist et al., 2009).
evidence: The introduction cites Gray et al., 2016 and Siegrist et al., 2009 to support the statement about ESX-3 function.

claim: The ESX-1 and ESX-4 systems of M. smegmatis are linked to DNA transfer.
source: Supporting this notion, ESX-3 of M. tuberculosis is required for mycobactin siderophore-based iron acquisition and the ESX-1 and ESX-4 systems of M. smegmatis are linked to DNA transfer (Gray et al., 2016; Siegrist et al., 2009).
evidence: The introduction cites Gray et al., 2016 and Siegrist et al., 2009 to support the statement about ESX-1 and ESX-4 function.

claim: A Staphylococcus aureus Esx-exported DNase toxin termed EssD (or EsaD) has been linked to virulence and contact-independent intraspecies antibacterial activity.
source: In Firmicutes, a Staphylococcus aureus Esx-exported DNase toxin termed EssD (or EsaD) has been linked to virulence and contact-independent intraspecies antibacterial activity (Cao et al., 2016; Ohr et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites Cao et al., 2016 and Ohr et al., 2017 to support the statement about EssD function.

claim: Esx secretion system genes are often linked to genes encoding polymorphic toxins belonging to the LXG protein family.
source: Aravind and colleagues have noted that Esx secretion system genes are often linked to genes encoding polymorphic toxins belonging to the LXG protein family (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites Zhang et al., 2012 to support the statement about genetic linkage.

claim: LXG proteins consist of a conserved N-terminal domain (LXG), a middle domain of variable length, and a C-terminal variable toxin domain.
source: Analogous to characteristic antimicrobial polymorphic toxins of Gram-negative bacteria, the LXG proteins consist of a conserved N-terminal domain (LXG), a middle domain of variable length, and a C-terminal variable toxin domain.
evidence: The introduction describes the domain structure of LXG proteins based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The LXG domain is predicted to adopt a structure resembling WXG100 proteins.
source: The LXG domain is predicted to adopt a structure resembling WXG100 proteins, thus leading to speculation that these proteins are Esx secretion system substrates (Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: The introduction cites Zhang et al., 2011 to support the prediction about LXG domain structure.

claim: There are no experimental data linking LXG proteins functionally to the Esx secretion system prior to this study.
source: Despite the association between LXG proteins and the Esx secretion system, to-date there are no experimental data linking them functionally.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states that no experimental data existed before this work.

claim: B. subtilis LXG RNase toxins exhibit antibacterial properties via heterologous expression in E. coli.
source: However, an intriguing study performed by Hayes and colleagues demonstrated antibacterial properties of B. subtilis LXG RNase toxins via heterologous expression in E. coli (Holberger et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites Holberger et al., 2012 to support the statement about B. subtilis LXG toxins.

claim: Growth inhibition by B. subtilis LXG RNase toxins was alleviated by co-expression of immunity determinants encoded adjacent to cognate LXG genes.
source: This growth inhibition was alleviated by co-expression of immunity determinants encoded adjacent to cognate LXG genes.
evidence: The introduction describes findings from Holberger et al., 2012 about immunity determinants.

claim: LXG proteins transit the Esx secretion system of Streptococcus intermedius.
source: We show here that LXG proteins transit the Esx secretion system of Streptococcus intermedius (Si) and function as antibacterial toxins that mediate contact-dependent interspecies antagonism.
evidence: The introduction states this as a finding of the study, supported by experimental data in the Results section.

claim: LXG proteins function as antibacterial toxins that mediate contact-dependent interspecies antagonism.
source: We show here that LXG proteins transit the Esx secretion system of Streptococcus intermedius (Si) and function as antibacterial toxins that mediate contact-dependent interspecies antagonism.
evidence: The introduction states this as a finding of the study, supported by experimental data in the Results section.

claim: The C-terminal domains in the LXG family members are highly divergent, exhibiting a wide range of predicted activities.
source: As noted previously, the C-terminal domains in the LXG family members we identified are highly divergent, exhibiting a wide range of predicted activities (Figure 1a) (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 1A showing diverse toxin domains, and cites Zhang et al., 2012.

claim: LXG protein-encoding genes are prevalent and broadly distributed in the classes Clostridiales, Bacillales and Lactobacillales.
source: LXG protein-encoding genes are prevalent and broadly distributed in the classes Clostridiales, Bacillales and Lactobacillales (Figure 1A).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 1A showing distribution across taxa.

claim: A significant proportion of organisms in Clostridiales, Bacillales and Lactobacillales are specifically adapted to the mammalian gut environment.
source: Notably, a significant proportion of organisms in these taxa are specifically adapted to the mammalian gut environment.
evidence: The Results section states this as established knowledge about these bacterial taxa.

claim: LXG genes derived from reference genomes of gut-adapted bacteria are abundant in metagenomic datasets from human gut microbiome samples.
source: Indeed, we find that LXG genes derived from reference genomes of many of these gut-adapted bacteria are abundant in metagenomic datasets from human gut microbiome samples (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Results section states this finding, supported by Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing metagenomic data.

claim: An LXG toxin predicted to possess ADP-ribosyltransferase activity was particularly abundant in a subset of human gut metagenomes.
source: An LXG toxin that is predicted to possess ADP-ribosyltransferase activity – previously linked to interbacterial antagonism in Gram-negative organisms – was particularly abundant in a subset of human gut metagenomes (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: The Results section states this observation from metagenomic analysis and cites Zhang et al., 2012.

claim: Close homologs of the ADP-ribosyltransferase LXG gene are found in Ruminococcus, a dominant taxa in the human gut microbiome.
source: Close homologs of this gene are found in Ruminococcus, a dominant taxa in the human gut microbiome, potentially explaining the frequency of this gene (Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: The Results section states this observation and cites Wu et al., 2011.

claim: The toxin domain of several LXG proteins shares homology and predicted catalytic residues with M. tuberculosis TNT, an NAD+-degrading (NADase) enzyme.
source: The toxin domain of several of the LXG proteins we identified shares homology and predicted catalytic residues with M. tuberculosis TNT, an NAD+-degrading (NADase) enzyme (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) (Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, and cites Sun et al., 2015.

claim: Si is a genetically tractable human commensal and opportunistic pathogen.
source: Si, a genetically tractable human commensal and opportunistic pathogen, is among the bacteria we identified that harbor a gene predicted to encode an NADase LXG protein (Claridge et al., 2001)
evidence: The Results section characterizes Si and cites Claridge et al., 2001.

claim: Induced expression of TelBtox* inhibited E. coli growth.
source: Induced expression of TelBtox* inhibited E. coli growth and reduced cellular NAD+ levels (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Induced expression of TelBtox* reduced cellular NAD+ levels in E. coli.
source: Induced expression of TelBtox* inhibited E. coli growth and reduced cellular NAD+ levels (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The extent of NAD+ depletion by TelBtox* mirrored that catalyzed by expression of Tse6, a previously characterized interbacterial NADase toxin.
source: The extent of NAD+ depletion mirrored that catalyzed by expression of a previously characterized interbacterial NADase toxin, Tse6, and importantly, intracellular NAD+ levels were unaffected by an unrelated bacteriostatic toxin, Tse2 (Hood et al., 2010; Whitney et al., 2015).
evidence: The Results section states this comparison and cites Hood et al., 2010 and Whitney et al., 2015.

claim: Intracellular NAD+ levels were unaffected by Tse2, an unrelated bacteriostatic toxin.
source: The extent of NAD+ depletion mirrored that catalyzed by expression of a previously characterized interbacterial NADase toxin, Tse6, and importantly, intracellular NAD+ levels were unaffected by an unrelated bacteriostatic toxin, Tse2 (Hood et al., 2010; Whitney et al., 2015).
evidence: The Results section states this observation and cites Hood et al., 2010 and Whitney et al., 2015.

claim: Substitution of R626A in TelB abrogated toxicity of TelBtox* and significantly restored NAD+ levels.
source: Furthermore, substitution of a second predicted catalytic residue of TelB (R626A), abrogated toxicity of TelBtox* and significantly restored NAD+ levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Concentrated cell-free supernatant of SiB196 possesses elevated levels of NADase activity relative to Si27335.
source: Using an assay that exploits fluorescent derivatives of NAD+ that form under strongly alkaline conditions, we found that concentrated cell-free supernatant of an Si strain containing telB (SiB196) possesses elevated levels of NADase activity relative to that of a strain lacking telB (Si27335) (Figure 2B) (Johnson and Morrison, 1970; Olson et al., 2013; Whiley and Beighton, 1991).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 2B, and cites Johnson and Morrison, 1970; Olson et al., 2013; Whiley and Beighton, 1991.

claim: The NADase activity present in the supernatant of SiB196 was abolished by telB inactivation.
source: Furthermore, the NADase activity present in the supernatant of SiB196 was abolished by telB inactivation.
evidence: The Results section states this observation from the NADase assay.

claim: Export of Esx substrates relies on EssC, a translocase with ATPase activity.
source: Export of Esx substrates relies on EssC, a translocase with ATPase activity (Burts et al., 2005; Rosenberg et al., 2015).
evidence: The Results section states this as established knowledge and cites Burts et al., 2005 and Rosenberg et al., 2015.

claim: Inactivation of essC abolished NADase activity in the supernatant of SiB196.
source: Inactivation of essC also abolished NADase activity in the supernatant of SiB196, suggesting that TelB utilizes the Esx pathway for export.
evidence: The Results section states this observation from the NADase assay.

claim: TelB utilizes the Esx pathway for export.
source: Inactivation of essC also abolished NADase activity in the supernatant of SiB196, suggesting that TelB utilizes the Esx pathway for export.
evidence: The Results section infers this from the essC-dependent secretion data.

claim: The genome of SiB196 encodes two additional LXG proteins, TelA and TelC.
source: The genome of SiB196 encodes two additional LXG proteins, which we named TelA and TelC (Figure 2C).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 2C showing the genomic organization.

claim: Each of the LXG proteins predicted by the Si genome is exported in an Esx-dependent manner.
source: This technique revealed that each of the LXG proteins predicted by the Si genome is exported in an Esx-dependent manner (Table 1).
evidence: The Results section states this finding, supported by Table 1 showing proteomic data.

claim: Western blot analysis of TelC secretion validated Esx-dependent export.
source: Western blot analysis of TelC secretion by wild-type and the essC-lacking mutant further validated Esx-dependent export (Figure 2D).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 2D showing Western blot data.

claim: LXG proteins are substrates of the Esx secretion system.
source: Together, these data indicate that LXG proteins are substrates of the Esx secretion system.
evidence: The Results section concludes this based on the secretion data presented.

claim: TelAtox and TelBtox* inhibited growth when expressed in the cytoplasm of E. coli.
source: TelAtox and TelBtox* inhibited growth when expressed in the cytoplasm of E. coli, whereas TelCtox did not exhibit toxicity in this cellular compartment (Figure 3A).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 3A showing toxicity assay data.

claim: TelCtox did not exhibit toxicity when expressed in the cytoplasm of E. coli.
source: TelAtox and TelBtox* inhibited growth when expressed in the cytoplasm of E. coli, whereas TelCtox did not exhibit toxicity in this cellular compartment (Figure 3A).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 3A showing toxicity assay data.

claim: Overexpression of ss-TelCtox (TelCtox with a signal peptide directing extracellular expression) exhibited significant toxicity in Si cells.
source: In contrast to TelCtox production, overexpression of a derivative bearing a signal peptide directing extracellular expression (ss-TelCtox) exhibited significant toxicity (Figure 3B).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 3B showing transformation efficiency data.

claim: A cognate tip (tel immunity protein) was identified for each toxin.
source: By co-expressing candidate open reading frames located downstream of each tel gene, we identified a cognate tip (tel immunity protein) for each toxin (Figure 3B–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Results section states this finding, supported by Figure 3B–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Wild-type SiB196 significantly inhibited the growth of TelB-susceptible strains in co-culture on solid surfaces.
source: We observed significant growth inhibition of TelB- or TelC-susceptible strains co-cultured with wild-type, but not when co-cultured with strains lacking telB or telC, respectively (Figure 3D).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 3D showing competition data.

claim: Wild-type SiB196 significantly inhibited the growth of TelC-susceptible strains in co-culture on solid surfaces.
source: We observed significant growth inhibition of TelB- or TelC-susceptible strains co-cultured with wild-type, but not when co-cultured with strains lacking telB or telC, respectively (Figure 3D).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 3D showing competition data.

claim: A strain bearing inactivated essC was unable to intoxicate a sensitive recipient.
source: A strain bearing inactivated essC was also unable to intoxicate a sensitive recipient.
evidence: The Results section states this observation from competition experiments.

claim: TelB and TelC-susceptible strains competed equally with wild type in liquid culture.
source: In competition experiments performed in parallel wherein the bacterial mixtures were grown in liquid culture, TelB and TelC-susceptible strains competed equally with wild type, suggesting that Esx-mediated intoxication requires prolonged cell contact.
evidence: The Results section states this observation from competition experiments.

claim: Esx-mediated intoxication requires prolonged cell contact.
source: In competition experiments performed in parallel wherein the bacterial mixtures were grown in liquid culture, TelB and TelC-susceptible strains competed equally with wild type, suggesting that Esx-mediated intoxication requires prolonged cell contact.
evidence: The Results section infers this from the difference between solid and liquid culture competition results.

claim: Physical separation of donor and recipient cells by a semi-permeable membrane blocked intoxication.
source: This physical separation blocked intoxication, which taken together with the results of our liquid co-culture experiments and our finding that purified TelC is not bactericidal, strongly suggests that the mechanism of Esx-dependent intercellular LXG protein delivery requires immediate cell-cell contact.
evidence: The Results section states this observation from filter-based competition experiments.

claim: The mechanism of Esx-dependent intercellular LXG protein delivery requires immediate cell-cell contact.
source: This physical separation blocked intoxication, which taken together with the results of our liquid co-culture experiments and our finding that purified TelC is not bactericidal, strongly suggests that the mechanism of Esx-dependent intercellular LXG protein delivery requires immediate cell-cell contact.
evidence: The Results section infers this from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The Esx pathway conferred fitness to SiB196 in competition with Si23775, S. pyogenes, and Enterococcus faecalis.
source: The Esx pathway conferred fitness to SiB196 in competition with Si23775, S. pyogenes, and Enterococcus faecalis, an organism from a closely related genus (Figure 3F).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 3F showing interspecies competition data.

claim: The Esx pathway did not measurably affect the competitiveness of SiB196 against Gram-negative species belonging to the phyla Proteobacteria or Bacteroidetes.
source: On the contrary, the pathway did not measurably affect the competitiveness of SiB196 against Gram-negative species belonging to the phyla Proteobacteria (E. coli, Burkholderia thailandensis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa) or Bacteroidetes (Bacteriodes fragilis).
evidence: The Results section states this observation from interspecies competition experiments.

claim: The Esx pathway can act between species.
source: These results demonstrate that the Esx pathway can act between species and suggest that its target range may be limited to Gram-positive bacteria.
evidence: The Results section concludes this based on the interspecies competition data.

claim: The target range of the Esx pathway may be limited to Gram-positive bacteria.
source: These results demonstrate that the Esx pathway can act between species and suggest that its target range may be limited to Gram-positive bacteria.
evidence: The Results section infers this from the differential effects on Gram-positive vs. Gram-negative targets.

claim: TelC contains a conserved aspartate-rich motif that constitutes its enzymatic active site.
source: This protein contains a conserved aspartate-rich motif that we hypothesized constitutes its enzymatic active site (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The Results section states this hypothesis, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1A showing sequence conservation.

claim: The crystal structure of TelCtox was determined to 2.0 Å resolution.
source: To gain further insight into TelC function, we determined the crystal structure of TelCtox to 2.0 Å resolution (Table 2).
evidence: The Results section states this, supported by Table 2 showing crystallographic statistics.

claim: The structure of TelCtox represents a new fold.
source: The structure of TelCtox represents a new fold; it is comprised of distinct and largely α-helical N- and C-terminal lobes (Figure 4A).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 4A showing the structure.

claim: TelCtox is comprised of distinct and largely α-helical N- and C-terminal lobes.
source: The structure of TelCtox represents a new fold; it is comprised of distinct and largely α-helical N- and C-terminal lobes (Figure 4A).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 4A showing the structure.

claim: The putative active site of TelCtox is located within a shallow groove that separates the N- and C-terminal lobes.
source: Although TelCtox does not share significant similarity to previously determined structures, we located its putative active site within a shallow groove that separates the N- and C-terminal lobes.
evidence: The Results section states this observation from structural analysis.

claim: The putative active site of TelCtox contains a calcium ion bound to several residues that comprise the conserved aspartate-rich motif.
source: This region contains a calcium ion bound to several residues that comprise the conserved aspartate-rich motif.
evidence: The Results section states this observation from the crystal structure.

claim: Site-specific mutagenesis of conserved aspartate residues abrogated TelC-based toxicity.
source: Site-specific mutagenesis of these residues abrogated TelC-based toxicity (Figure 4B,C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 4B,C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: S. aureus cells expressing extracellularly-targeted TelCtox exhibited significantly reduced viability.
source: S. aureus cells expressing extracellularly-targeted TelCtox exhibited significantly reduced viability (Figure 4D)
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 4D showing viability data.

claim: S. aureus cells expressing ss-TelCtox displayed a cessation of cell growth followed by lysis.
source: and when examined microscopically, displayed a cessation of cell growth followed by lysis that was not observed in control cells (Figure 4E, Videos 1–2).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 4E and Videos 1–2 showing microscopy data.

claim: Isolated cell walls treated with TelCtox showed no evidence of enzymatic digestion.
source: Despite eliciting effects consistent with cell wall peptidoglycan disruption, isolated cell walls treated with TelCtox and peptidoglycan recovered from cells undergoing TelC-based intoxication showed no evidence of enzymatic digestion (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D showing HPLC data.

claim: Peptidoglycan recovered from cells undergoing TelC-based intoxication showed no evidence of enzymatic digestion.
source: Despite eliciting effects consistent with cell wall peptidoglycan disruption, isolated cell walls treated with TelCtox and peptidoglycan recovered from cells undergoing TelC-based intoxication showed no evidence of enzymatic digestion (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D showing HPLC data.

claim: TelC corrupts peptidoglycan biosynthesis.
source: These data prompted us to consider that TelC corrupts peptidoglycan biosynthesis, which could also lead to the lytic phenotype observed (Harkness and Braun, 1989).
evidence: The Results section infers this mechanism and cites Harkness and Braun, 1989.

claim: Lipid II is the immediate precursor of peptidoglycan.
source: The immediate precursor of peptidoglycan is lipid II, which consists of the oligopeptide disaccharide repeat unit linked via pyrophosphate to a lipid carrier (Vollmer and Bertsche, 2008).
evidence: The Results section states this as established knowledge and cites Vollmer and Bertsche, 2008.

claim: Lipid II is the target of diverse antibacterial molecules.
source: Likely due to its distinctive and conserved structure, lipid II is the target of diverse antibacterial molecules (Breukink and de Kruijff, 2006; Oppedijk et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section states this as established knowledge and cites Breukink and de Kruijff, 2006 and Oppedijk et al., 2016.

claim: TelCtox cleaves lipid II at the phosphoester linkage to undecaprenyl.
source: Analysis of the reaction products showed that TelCtox cleaves lipid II – severing the molecule at the phosphoester linkage to undecaprenyl (Figure 4F–G, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 4F–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A showing TLC and HPLC data.

claim: Reaction products of TelCtox-mediated lipid II cleavage were confirmed by mass spectrometry.
source: Reaction products were confirmed by mass spectrometry and inclusion of TipC inhibited their formation.
evidence: The Results section states this observation from mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Inclusion of TipC inhibited the formation of lipid II cleavage products by TelCtox.
source: Reaction products were confirmed by mass spectrometry and inclusion of TipC inhibited their formation.
evidence: The Results section states this observation from biochemical assays.

claim: Consumption of lipid II for peptidoglycan assembly generates undecaprenyl pyrophosphate (UPP), which is converted to undecaprenyl phosphate (UP).
source: Consumption of lipid II for peptidoglycan assembly generates undecaprenyl pyrophosphate (UPP), which is converted to undecaprenyl phosphate (UP), and transported inside the cell.
evidence: The Results section states this as established knowledge about peptidoglycan biosynthesis.

claim: UP reenters peptidoglycan biosynthesis or is utilized as a carrier for wall teichoic acid (WTA).
source: The UP molecule then reenters peptidoglycan biosynthesis or is utilized as a carrier for another essential cell wall constituent, wall teichoic acid (WTA).
evidence: The Results section states this as established knowledge about cell wall biosynthesis.

claim: TelCtox is capable of hydrolyzing cleaved undecaprenyl derivatives but displays a strict requirement for the pyrophosphate group.
source: Our experiments showed that TelCtox is capable of hydrolyzing cleaved undecaprenyl derivatives but displays a strict requirement for the pyrophosphate group (Figure 4H)
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 4H showing TLC data.

claim: TelC has the potential to simultaneously disrupt two critical Gram-positive cell wall polymers (peptidoglycan and wall teichoic acid).
source: indicating the potential for TelC to simultaneously disrupt two critical Gram-positive cell wall polymers.
evidence: The Results section infers this from the substrate specificity data.

claim: TelC exhibited toxicity towards diverse Gram-positive species including Si, S. aureus and E. faecalis.
source: Consistent with its ability to inhibit a conserved step in peptidoglycan biosynthesis, TelC exhibited toxicity towards diverse Gram-positive species including Si (Figure 2B), S. aureus (Figure 4D) and E. faecalis (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by multiple figures showing toxicity data.

claim: TelC expression in the cytoplasm or secretory pathway of yeast does not impact the viability of this model eukaryotic cell.
source: While we cannot rule out that TelC may have other targets, we find that its expression in the cytoplasm or secretory pathway of yeast does not impact the viability of this model eukaryotic cell (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C–D).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 3C–D showing yeast viability data.

claim: telB- and telC-inactivated strains of Si retain the capacity to secrete TelC and TelB, respectively.
source: Using Western blot analysis to measure TelC secretion and extracellular NADase activity as a proxy for TelB secretion, we found that telB- and telC-inactivated strains of Si retain the capacity to secrete TelC and TelB, respectively (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 5A–B showing secretion data.

claim: TelB and TelC are not required for core Esx apparatus function and do not display secretion co-dependency.
source: These data indicate that TelB and TelC are not required for core apparatus function and do not display secretion co-dependency.
evidence: The Results section concludes this based on the secretion data.

claim: Genes encoding WXG100-like proteins are located upstream of telA-C (wxgA-C).
source: Interestingly, we noted genes encoding WXG100-like proteins upstream of telA-C (wxgA-C) (Figure 2C)
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 2C showing genomic organization.

claim: WXG100-like proteins (WxgA-C) were not identified in the extracellular proteome of Si.
source: however, these proteins were not identified in the extracellular proteome of Si (Table 1).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Table 1 showing proteomic data.

claim: WxgC, but not WxgB, co-purified with TelC.
source: In support of this, we found that WxgC, but not WxgB co-purified with TelC (Figure 5C).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 5C showing co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: The interaction between WxgC and TelC is mediated by the LXG domain of TelC.
source: Moreover, using bacterial two-hybrid assays, we determined that this interaction is mediated by the LXG domain of TelC (Figure 5D).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 5D showing bacterial two-hybrid data.

claim: WxgA-C interact specifically with the LXG domain of their cognate toxins.
source: We found that WxgA-C interact specifically with the LXG domain of their cognate toxins (Figure 5D).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 5D showing bacterial two-hybrid data.

claim: wxgC inactivation abrogates TelC secretion, but not that of TelB.
source: We found that wxgC inactivation abrogates TelC secretion, but not that of TelB (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: The Results section states this observation, supported by Figure 5A–B showing secretion data.

claim: Cognate Tel–Wxg interaction facilitates secretion through the Esx pathway of Si.
source: In summary, these data suggest that cognate Tel–Wxg interaction facilitates secretion through the Esx pathway of Si (Figure 5E).
evidence: The Results section concludes this based on the interaction and secretion data, supported by Figure 5E showing a model.

claim: Esx-mediated delivery of LXG toxins serves as a physiological mechanism for interbacterial antagonism between Gram-positive bacteria.
source: We present multiple lines of evidence that Esx-mediated delivery of LXG toxins serves as a physiological mechanism for interbacterial antagonism between Gram-positive bacteria.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: The Esx system may mediate antagonism against diverse targets, ranging from related strains to species belonging to other genera.
source: Our results suggest that like the T6S pathway of Gram-negative bacteria, the Esx system may mediate antagonism against diverse targets, ranging from related strains to species belonging to other genera (Schwarz et al., 2010).
evidence: The Discussion infers this from the competition data and cites Schwarz et al., 2010.

claim: The Esx system could have significant ramifications for the composition of human-associated polymicrobial communities.
source: This feature of Esx secretion, in conjunction with the frequency by which we detect LXG genes in human gut metagenomes, suggests that the system could have significant ramifications for the composition of human-associated polymicrobial communities.
evidence: The Discussion speculates about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: LXG toxins may assist Listeria in colonizing fermented food communities dominated by Lactobacillus and Lactococcus.
source: For instance, LXG toxins may assist Listeria in colonizing fermented food communities dominated by Lactobacillus and Lactococcus (Farber and Peterkin, 1991).
evidence: The Discussion speculates about the role of LXG toxins in food microbiology and cites Farber and Peterkin, 1991.

claim: Lactobacillus and Lactococcus genera possess LXG toxins, which may augment their known antimicrobial properties.
source: Of note, the latter genera also possess LXG toxins, which may augment their known antimicrobial properties.
evidence: The Discussion speculates about the function of LXG toxins in these genera.

claim: The relationship between S. aureus EssD and the LXG toxins reported in this study is currently unclear.
source: Palmer and colleagues recently reported that the Esx system of Staphylococcus aureus exports EssD, a nuclease capable of inhibiting the growth of target bacteria in co-culture (Cao et al., 2016). The relationship between these findings and those we report herein is currently unclear.
evidence: The Discussion acknowledges uncertainty about the relationship between different findings and cites Cao et al., 2016.

claim: S. aureus EssD does not possess an LXG domain.
source: S. aureus EssD does not possess an LXG domain and was reported to be active against susceptible bacteria during co-incubation in liquid media, a condition we found not conducive to LXG toxin delivery (Figure 3D).
evidence: The Discussion compares EssD to LXG toxins based on domain structure and activity conditions.

claim: The Esx pathway is functionally pliable.
source: It is evident that the Esx pathway is functionally pliable (Burts et al., 2005; Conrad et al., 2017; Gray et al., 2016; Gröschel et al., 2016; Manzanillo et al., 2012; Siegrist et al., 2009)
evidence: The Discussion states this as established knowledge and cites multiple references.

claim: The Esx pathway may target toxins to bacteria through multiple mechanisms.
source: therefore, it is conceivable that it targets toxins to bacteria through multiple mechanisms.
evidence: The Discussion speculates about the diversity of Esx-mediated mechanisms.

claim: LXG proteins require hetero-dimerization with specific WXG100-like partners to be secreted.
source: Our data suggest that, like a subset of substrates of the Esx systems of M. tuberculosis, LXG family members require hetero-dimerization with specific WXG100-like partners to be secreted (Ates et al., 2016).
evidence: The Discussion infers this from the interaction and secretion data and cites Ates et al., 2016.

claim: Hetero-dimerization is thought to facilitate secretion of Esx substrates due to the requirement for a bipartite secretion signal.
source: Hetero-dimerization is thought to facilitate secretion of these substrates due to the requirement for a bipartite secretion signal consisting of a YxxxD/E motif in the C-terminus of one partner in proximity to the WXG motif present in the turn between helices in the second protein (Champion et al., 2006; Daleke et al., 2012a; Poulsen et al., 2014; Sysoeva et al., 2014).
evidence: The Discussion states this as established knowledge and cites multiple references.

claim: WxgA-C could function analogously to the EspG proteins of M. tuberculosis, which serve as intracellular chaperones.
source: This suggests that WxgA-C could function analogously to the EspG proteins of M. tuberculosis, which serve as intracellular chaperones facilitating delivery of specific substrates to the secretion machinery (Daleke et al., 2012b; Ekiert and Cox, 2014).
evidence: The Discussion speculates about the function of Wxg proteins and cites Daleke et al., 2012b and Ekiert and Cox, 2014.

claim: Wxg–Lxg complexes could be secreted as heterodimers, but the Wxg member was undetected for technical reasons.
source: Alternatively, Wxg–Lxg complexes could be secreted as heterodimers, but for technical reasons the Wxg member was undetected in our experiments.
evidence: The Discussion speculates about an alternative explanation for the data.

claim: The paradigm of Lxg-Wxg interaction likely extends beyond S. intermedius.
source: The paradigm of Lxg-Wxg interaction likely extends beyond S. intermedius, as we observe that LXG proteins from other species are commonly encoded within the same operon as Wxg homologs.
evidence: The Discussion infers this from genomic organization data.

claim: The size of LXG toxins exceeds that of molecules capable of free diffusion across the peptidoglycan sacculus.
source: The size of LXG toxins exceeds that of molecules capable of free diffusion across the peptidoglycan sacculus (Forster and Marquis, 2012).
evidence: The Discussion states this based on established knowledge and cites Forster and Marquis, 2012.

claim: Donor cell-derived cell wall hydrolytic enzymes may facilitate entry of LXG toxins.
source: Donor cell-derived cell wall hydrolytic enzymes may facilitate entry or the LXG proteins could exploit cell surface proteins present on recipient cells.
evidence: The Discussion speculates about mechanisms of toxin entry.

claim: LXG proteins could exploit cell surface proteins present on recipient cells.
source: Donor cell-derived cell wall hydrolytic enzymes may facilitate entry or the LXG proteins could exploit cell surface proteins present on recipient cells.
evidence: The Discussion speculates about mechanisms of toxin entry.

claim: The requirement for donor-recipient cell contact may reflect a step subsequent to secretion by the Esx pathway.
source: Whether the entry of LXG toxins is directly coordinated by the Esx pathway is not known; our experiments do not rule-out that the requirement for donor-recipient cell contact reflects a step subsequent to secretion by the Esx pathway.
evidence: The Discussion acknowledges limitations in interpreting the contact-dependence data.

claim: The central domain of TelA and TelB may participate in toxin entry.
source: Our study has identified roles for the N- and C-terminal domains of LXG proteins; however, the function of the region between these two domains remains undefined and may participate in entry.
evidence: The Discussion speculates about the function of the central domain.

claim: The central domains of TelA and TelB are each over 150 residues, whereas the LXG and toxin domains of TelC appear to directly fuse.
source: Intriguingly, the central domains of TelA and TelB are each over 150 residues, whereas the LXG and toxin domains of TelC, which does not require access to the cytoplasm, appear to directly fuse (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Discussion states this observation, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing domain boundaries.

claim: TelC adopts a previously unobserved fold.
source: We discovered that TelC, a protein lacking characterized homologs, adopts a previously unobserved fold and catalyzes degradation of the cell wall precursor molecule lipid II.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the structural finding.

claim: TelC catalyzes degradation of the cell wall precursor molecule lipid II.
source: We discovered that TelC, a protein lacking characterized homologs, adopts a previously unobserved fold and catalyzes degradation of the cell wall precursor molecule lipid II.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the biochemical finding.

claim: Lipid II is the target of the food preservative nisin.
source: This molecule is the target of the food preservative nisin, as well as the last-line antibiotic vancomycin, which is used to treat a variety of Gram-positive infections (Ng and Chan, 2016).
evidence: The Discussion states this as established knowledge and cites Ng and Chan, 2016.

claim: Lipid II is the target of the last-line antibiotic vancomycin.
source: This molecule is the target of the food preservative nisin, as well as the last-line antibiotic vancomycin, which is used to treat a variety of Gram-positive infections (Ng and Chan, 2016).
evidence: The Discussion states this as established knowledge and cites Ng and Chan, 2016.

claim: Lipid II is the target of the antibiotic teixobactin, synthesized by the soil bacterium Eleftheria terrae.
source: Lipid II is also the target of the recently discovered antibiotic teixobactin, synthesized by the soil bacterium Eleftheria terrae (Ling et al., 2015).
evidence: The Discussion states this and cites Ling et al., 2015.

claim: Teixobactin has a low rate at which resistance is evolved.
source: A particularly interesting property of this potential therapeutic is the low rate at which resistance is evolved.
evidence: The Discussion states this property of teixobactin.

claim: The challenge of structurally modifying lipid II may explain why interbacterial toxins targeting this molecule have evolved independently in Gram-negative (colicin M) and -positive (TelC) bacteria.
source: The apparent challenge of structurally modifying lipid II in order to subvert antimicrobials may explain why interbacterial toxins targeting this molecule have evolved independently in Gram-negative (colicin M) and -positive (TelC) bacteria (El Ghachi et al., 2006).
evidence: The Discussion speculates about the evolutionary significance of lipid II-targeting toxins and cites El Ghachi et al., 2006.

claim: Biochemical characterization of additional LXG toxins of unknown function will reveal further Gram-positive cell vulnerabilities that could be exploited in the design of new antibiotics.
source: We anticipate that biochemical characterization of additional LXG toxins of unknown function will reveal further Gram-positive cell vulnerabilities that could likewise be exploited in the design of new antibiotics.
evidence: The Discussion speculates about future applications of this research.
